analysis.one_liner: Extends ACA premium subsidies for two years, but adds a $5 minimum premium, citizen-only eligibility, and an abortion-coverage ban.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced December 9, 2025 with zero cosponsors, has sat in the Senate Finance Committee ever since, while the enhanced premium credits it would extend are scheduled to lapse at the end of 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would extend the enhanced Affordable Care Act premium tax credits — set to expire after 2025 — through 2027, then keep a scaled-back version permanently for households earning up to six times the poverty line. It would require every enrollee to pay at least $5 a month, limit credits and cost-sharing help to U.S. citizens only, and bar marketplace plans from covering abortion. It would also restore federal funding for cost-sharing reductions, which lower deductibles for lower-income enrollees, starting in 2027.
analysis.who_benefits: Marketplace enrollees — especially households above the old 400%-of-poverty cutoff and lower-income families whose premiums would jump when the enhanced credits lapse after 2025 — would keep subsidies for two more years and a capped version after that. Health insurers also gain: subsidies would keep flowing to their plans, and direct federal cost-sharing payments to them would resume in 2027.

how_it_helps.text: It would extend the enhanced premium tax credits through 2027, preventing the large premium increases marketplace enrollees would face when the current expansion runs out after 2025.

Instead of returning to the old 400%-of-poverty cutoff, it would keep a version of the enhanced credit permanently for households up to 600% of poverty, with required premium contributions capped on a sliding scale from 8.5% to 16.5% of income.
It would restore federal appropriations for cost-sharing reductions — payments that lower deductibles and copays for lower-income marketplace enrollees — for plan years starting in 2027.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers would fund the extended credits and the newly appropriated cost-sharing payments. Lawfully present immigrants would lose premium credits and cost-sharing help entirely; marketplace enrollees would lose abortion coverage; and the lowest-income enrollees would start paying $5 a month where many currently pay nothing.

drawbacks.text: Beginning after 2025, only U.S. citizens could receive premium credits and cost-sharing help, cutting off lawfully present immigrants — including green card holders and people working in the country legally — who qualify today.

Any marketplace plan that covers abortion could no longer be a qualified health plan, except for cases of rape, incest, or danger to the mother's life — so enrollees could not buy a marketplace plan that includes abortion coverage even with their own money.
Every enrollee would owe at least $5 a month in premiums, ending the $0-premium plans millions of the lowest-income households have now.

After 2027 the enhanced credit would be capped at 600% of the poverty line, so households above that line would lose all help, and those between 400% and 600% would pay more than under the current unlimited enhanced credits.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The subsidy extension is a real benefit — without it, millions of marketplace enrollees face steep premium increases in 2026. But the bill buys that extension by cutting legal immigrants out of the program, banning abortion coverage from marketplace plans altogether, and charging the poorest enrollees a minimum premium. It also only extends the full enhanced credits for two years before phasing them into a 600%-of-poverty cap, setting up another affordability cliff in 2028. Whether that trade is worth it depends heavily on how much weight a reader puts on the restrictions versus the extension itself.

outcome.mechanism: The bill has sat in the Senate Finance Committee since it was introduced in December 2025, with no hearing, no vote, and no cosponsors.

narrative.text: Sen. Jon Husted introduced the bill on December 9, 2025; it was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which sets tax policy.
No other senator from either party signed on as a cosponsor.
The action history shows nothing after the referral — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote.
Meanwhile, the enhanced premium credits the bill would extend are scheduled to expire after 2025, so marketplace premiums are set to rise without congressional action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has moved the credits either way: the expiration remains on schedule and no extension — this one or any other — has been enacted. The delay benefits anyone who wants the credits to lapse or to return only with stricter conditions, and it leaves enrollees facing 2026 premium increases with no fix.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Supporters of letting the credits lapse, for now

for.name: Sen. Jon Husted
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on December 9, 2025, proposing a two-year extension of the enhanced premium credits paired with citizenship, minimum-premium, and abortion-coverage restrictions.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee (Chair Mike Crapo)
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over the bill
against.what_they_did: Took no action after the December 9, 2025 referral — no hearing, markup, or vote appears in the action history.

against.name: Senate Democratic leadership
against.what_they_did: Pushed for an unconditional extension of the enhanced credits and did not accept conditions like citizenship-only eligibility or abortion restrictions in end-of-2025 negotiations over the lapsing subsidies.

sides.party_line_note: No votes have occurred; the bill's only sponsor is a Republican and it has drawn no cosponsors from either party, so its partisan shape is untested.

industries.industry: Health insurers selling ACA marketplace plans
industries.note: The bill keeps federal premium subsidies flowing through private marketplace plans for at least two more years and restores direct cost-sharing payments to insurers starting in 2027, locking in insurers' role as the delivery channel for federal health aid. Insurers and enrollees both benefit from the extension here, though the citizenship rule trims a small slice of their customer base.

analysis.trajectory: With the enhanced credits lapsing after 2025, Congress faces pressure to act in early 2026, and versions of this proposal could be folded into a larger deal. But with zero cosponsors and no committee action, the bill is unlikely to advance on its own; its restrictions — citizenship-only eligibility, the $5 minimum premium, the abortion ban — are more likely to reappear as Republican conditions in any extension negotiation.
